title: Quotes inside quotes
brief:
A string can be written between double quotes `"like this"` or single quotes `'like this'`. Usually it does not matter which you choose. It matters when the text itself contains a quote mark.

If your text contains an apostrophe, such as didn't, wrap the string in double quotes. If your text contains double quotes, such as say "hi", wrap the string in single quotes. Otherwise Python thinks the string ends early and you get a SyntaxError.

Print these two lines exactly: first `no, you didn't` and then `say "hi" to the rover`.

vocabulary.gloss: a piece of text, written between quotes: `"hello"` or `'10'`.
the `print()` function writes text to the terminal (the screen).
the text of a program, written by a programmer.

starterCode:
"""
File: quotes.py
---------------
Printing text that contains quote marks.
"""


def main():
    pass


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

tests.expectedStdout:
no, you didn't
say "hi" to the rover

reflect: When do you use single quotes and when double quotes? Give one example of each.
solution:
"""
File: quotes.py
---------------
Printing text that contains quote marks.
"""


def main():
    print("no, you didn't")
    print('say "hi" to the rover')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
